domain: deep-time geology and natural history of Washington State (Precambrian to present, plus a qualitative 50 Ma projection), compiled for the place-history site's outer rings (Washington / Cascadia) with Seattle and Puget Lowland depth
caveats: AGES: start_years_ago/end_years_ago are years before 2000 CE (2000 - year for CE dates; the 2001 Nisqually quake is -1; the 50 Ma projection is -50,000,000, i.e. in the future). Ice-age ages are given in CALENDAR (calibrated) years where the literature supports it; older papers (Thorson 1980, Waitt 1983, Sea-Tac sloth 1961 dates) report radiocarbon years that are 1,500-2,500 years younger than calendar years, which explains why popular sources disagree (e.g. Vashon maximum '14,000' vs '17,000' years ago). Where sources disagree the summary gives the range and confidence is lowered. PLACEHOLDERS used in at_your_spot templates: {place} = the visitor's spot/ring name; {ice_thickness} = ice thickness interpolated from Thorson (1980) contours (approx. 5,000 ft Bellingham, 3,000 ft Seattle, 2,000 ft Tacoma, ~1,000 ft Olympia, ~660 ft at the Tenino terminus); {basalt_unit} / {basalt_thickness} from DNR 100K geology units of the Columbia River Basalt Group; {flood_depth} = Lake Lewis level (1,200-1,250 ft) minus ground elevation, or DNR unit Qfg presence; {nearest_volcano} and {distance_mi} from DNR Volcanic_Vents; {elevation_ft} from a DEM or the geocoder; {county} from the county ring. The site must decide applicability per ring: an event's 'region' says where it applies, but Missoula-flood and Lake Lewis sentences should only be shown if the spot is in the Channeled Scabland/Pasco-Quincy-Yakima-Walla Walla basins below ~1,250 ft (DNR unit Qfg or the Ice Age Floods extent), Vashon sentences only north of the Tenino ice limit, Osceola/Electron sentences only in the mapped lahar deposits (USGS/DNR lahar hazard layers), CRBG sentences only where DNR map units are CRBG members (roughly 36% of the state). LICENSING: USGS, NPS and WA DNR text and images are public domain / open; HistoryLink is link-out only (no API, text is copyrighted - summarize, do not copy); Burke Museum pages are copyrighted (link out); Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA (attribute if quoted). KNOWN CONFLICTS: Cascades uplift onset (10 Ma USGS table vs 4-7 Ma Burke/others); Olympic emergence (34 Ma NPS 'began rising' vs 18 Ma DNR vs 16.5-13.3 Ma Lithosphere 2020); Withrow Moraine age (22-18, 17.5-17, or 15.4 ka by different methods); 1949 magnitude (Mw 7.1 HistoryLink/USGS older vs 6.7 Wikipedia) and 1965 (6.7 vs 6.5); 1872 magnitude (6.5-7.0, best 6.8) and epicenter (Entiat/south Lake Chelan); Seattle Fault 923-924 CE magnitude (7.0-7.5 single fault, up to 7.8 if Seattle + Saddle Mountain faults ruptured together); Lake Lewis elevation 1,200 vs 1,250 ft; Tacoma and Olympia ice thickness come from a single secondary source and should be shown as 'about'. The Sea-Tac sloth and Ayer Pond bison dates are radiocarbon ages converted to approximate calendar ages by me, not by the cited sources. The 50 Ma projection is speculative by nature (low confidence): no peer-reviewed source gives a date for the end of Juan de Fuca subduction. Washington's 'oldest rock' is a moving target: a 2024 USGS field guide argues some strata mapped as Belt are younger (<1,360 Ma Deer Trail Group); the 1.47-1.40 Ga Belt age is still the standard public figure (WA DNR/WA100). Events not in the brief but added because visitors in those places would expect them: Rodinia rifting/Windermere, Cambrian Metaline seas (NE WA), Eocene Okanogan core complexes (folded into Stonerose), the Okanogan lobe/Glacial Lake Columbia/Grand Coulee, pre-Vashon glaciations, the birth of Puget Sound, the birth of the modern volcanoes, and ice-age megafauna beyond Manis. Not covered (out of scope for the deep-time ring): Holocene sea-level history, the Lake Washington ship-canal lowering, Seattle regrades and tideflat fills.

events.title: Washington's oldest rocks: the Belt Supergroup
events.summary: The oldest rocks you can touch in Washington are mudstones, sandstones and limy layers of the Belt Supergroup in the state's far northeast corner (Pend Oreille and Stevens counties, Colville National Forest). They settled in a vast, shallow inland basin on the ancient continent of Laurentia when the only life was microbial - stromatolite mounds built by cyanobacteria are preserved in them. Some ten miles of these sediments bury an even older continental basement that never reaches the surface in Washington; rocks of about 2.5 billion years crop out just across the Idaho line.

events.title: Rodinia breaks apart: North America's new western edge
events.summary: When the supercontinent Rodinia rifted apart, the piece that became North America was left with a brand-new western coastline running roughly through today's northeastern Washington. Rift-valley gravels and glacial debris of the Windermere Group (about 700 million years old) record that break-up and a global 'Snowball Earth' cold spell. Everything west of this line - most of the state - did not exist yet; it would arrive piece by piece over the next half-billion years.

events.title: Warm Cambrian seas: the Metaline limestone and Gardner Cave
events.summary: Northeastern Washington was the continental shelf of North America, under a warm shallow sea where shells and reef debris piled up into more than 3,000 feet of Metaline limestone, capped by black Ordovician slate. Trilobites and graptolites are its fossils. That limestone later hosted the Pend Oreille zinc-lead mines and, dissolved by rainwater, Gardner Cave - Washington's longest limestone cave, in Crawford State Park near Metaline Falls.

events.title: Island arcs dock: Quesnellia and the Okanogan Highlands
events.summary: The first big piece of 'new' Washington arrived in the Jurassic: Quesnellia, a volcanic island arc that had been growing offshore since the Mississippian, was shoved onto the old continental edge. The collision squeezed and lifted the Kootenay Arc (about 160 million years ago) and set the stage for huge granite bodies such as the Cretaceous Okanogan Batholith. Much later, in the Eocene (56-34 million years ago), the crust here stretched and the Okanogan and Kettle dome-and-basin landscape formed.

events.title: The North Cascades, Methow and San Juan terranes are welded on
events.when: about 100 to 84 million years ago (mid-Late Cretaceous), building on Jurassic pieces
events.summary: Long-running subduction dragged a jumble of exotic crust - ocean floor, island arcs, deep-sea sediments - against the continent. The San Juan Islands and the Northwest Cascades are stacked thrust sheets of such terranes, pinned down before about 84 million years ago by the overlying Nanaimo Group sediments; the Methow Valley records island-arc and ocean-floor terranes docking in the middle and late Cretaceous; and the North Cascades crystalline core was cooked and squeezed at depth into the gneisses seen at Stehekin and Washington Pass. Paleomagnetic data suggest some of these blocks formed up to a thousand miles to the south and slid north along the coast.

events.title: Siletzia: a volcanic ocean plateau collides and becomes western Washington's basement
events.when: eruptions 56-48 million years ago; collision 51-50 million years ago (early Eocene)
events.summary: An enormous pile of submarine basalt - Siletzia, possibly built over the young Yellowstone hotspot - rode in on the Farallon plate and jammed against North America about 51-50 million years ago, too thick to subduct. Its Washington part is the Crescent Formation: pillow lavas that now form the horseshoe of ridges around the Olympic Mountains (Hurricane Ridge road cuts), the Black Hills and Willapa Hills, and the hidden basement beneath Seattle, Tacoma and the whole Puget Lowland. The collision ended the old coastline, folded the Chuckanut and Swauk basins, and reset the subduction zone to roughly its present position.

events.title: Eocene palm forests and coal swamps: Chuckanut, Swauk and the Puget Group
events.when: about 57 to 38 million years ago (late Paleocene to late Eocene)
events.summary: Western Washington was a steamy, subtropical river plain. Fan palms, tree ferns and swamp cypresses grew along braided rivers that laid down the Chuckanut Formation around Bellingham (fossil palm fronds and the tracks of the giant flightless bird Diatryma at Racehorse Creek), the Swauk Formation near Blewett Pass, and later the Puget Group of the Seattle area. Peat from those swamps became the coal that built Newcastle, Renton, Black Diamond, Issaquah and Roslyn in the 1800s. Cooling late in the Eocene drove the palms out for good.
events.at_your_spot: About 50 million years ago {place} was a hot, humid river floodplain with palms and tree ferns; the coal under the Eastside and the Cle Elum valley is the remains of those swamps.

events.title: Stonerose: the Republic fossil lake
events.summary: As the crust of the Okanogan Highlands stretched apart (53-45 million years ago), a deep upland lake filled the Republic graben. Its fine lakebed shales - the Klondike Mountain Formation, dated 49.4 +/- 0.5 million years - preserve one of the world's finest Eocene floras: dawn redwood, sassafras, early relatives of roses, maples and apples, plus insects, fish and feathers. At the Stonerose Interpretive Center in Republic, visitors can dig their own fossils (important finds stay in the research collection; the Burke Museum holds a major collection too).

events.title: The Cascade volcanic arc switches on
events.when: about 40-37 million years ago, and still active
events.summary: Once Siletzia had reset the plate boundary, the sinking ocean plate began feeding magma to a new line of volcanoes - the ancestral Cascades - starting about 40-37 million years ago (DNR gives 43-37). Early vents punched through shallow seas and coastal plains in southwest Washington; their ash and lava (the Ohanapecosh and Stevens Ridge formations) make up the foundations of Mount Rainier National Park. The volcanoes we see today are only the newest instalments of this 40-million-year arc.

events.title: Columbia River Basalt floods bury a third of Washington
events.when: about 16.7 to 6 million years ago (Miocene); 90% erupted 16.5-15.6 Ma
events.summary: From fissures in southeast Washington and adjacent Oregon and Idaho - probably fed by the Yellowstone hotspot - more than 300 floods of basalt lava poured out, each filling the landscape like water in a basin. The flows cover over 80,000 square miles across three states and about 36% of Washington: everything from Spokane, Pullman, Walla Walla and the Tri-Cities to Yakima, Moses Lake, Wenatchee's east side and Goldendale, stacked up to two miles thick under the Pasco Basin. Some flows ran down the Columbia River Gorge to Vancouver and all the way to the Pacific. The Puget Lowland, Olympics, North Cascades and the northeast highlands were never buried. Later folding of the cooled basalt made the Yakima ridges.

events.title: Ginkgo Petrified Forest at Vantage
events.summary: Between basalt floods, a lake and swampy forest grew where the Columbia now cuts through at Vantage. When the next lava (the Ginkgo flow of the Wanapum Basalt) poured in, waterlogged logs - ginkgo, Douglas-fir, spruce, elm, sweetgum, walnut and more than 50 species in all - were sealed under lava and slowly turned to stone. George Beck of Ellensburg recognized the deposit in the 1930s; it is now Ginkgo Petrified Forest State Park, and petrified wood is Washington's state gem.

events.title: The Blue Lake Rhino
events.when: about 15 million years ago (middle Miocene); discovered July 1935
events.summary: A rhinoceros (Diceratherium) lying dead in a shallow lake was engulfed by a basalt flow; the water chilled the lava into pillows around the carcass and left a rhino-shaped cavity in the rock. In July 1935 fossil hunters scrambling along the cliffs of Jasper Canyon at the east end of Blue Lake, in the lower Grand Coulee, found the cave with bone fragments and a jaw inside. A cast of the cavity is displayed at the Burke Museum; the cave itself is a strenuous, unmarked scramble in Sun Lakes-Dry Falls State Park.

events.title: The Olympic Mountains rise from the sea
events.when: wedge building since ~45 Ma; land emerges about 18-13 million years ago; still rising
events.summary: The Olympics are not volcanoes: they are deep-sea sandstones and shales scraped off the sinking Juan de Fuca plate and stuffed under the rim of Siletzia basalt, then squeezed upward. Sediment studies show the peninsula first broke the sea surface about 16.5-13 million years ago (DNR says the rise began around 18 Ma), and the range has been lifting - and eroding just as fast - ever since. The Hurricane Ridge fault is the seam between the core sandstones and the basalt rim; Mount Olympus (7,980 ft) is the high point.

events.title: The Cascade Range is lifted to its modern height
events.when: roughly 12 to 4 million years ago (late Miocene-Pliocene)
events.summary: For most of their history the Cascades were a belt of volcanoes on low ground, with lavas and ash spilling east onto the basalt plateau. Then the whole range was pushed up as a block: rock-cooling studies show rapid uplift and erosion in Washington 12-8 million years ago, and the Burke Museum places the final rise of the modern range at 4-7 million years ago. The rain shadow that makes eastern Washington dry, and the river canyons that cut the range, date from this time.

events.title: The modern volcanoes are born: Adams, Rainier, St. Helens, Baker
events.when: about 520,000 to 140,000 years ago (and still active)
events.summary: The peaks on today's skyline are young. Mount Adams began erupting about 520,000 years ago; the present Mount Rainier started building about 500,000 years ago on the stump of an older volcano; Mount St. Helens' first eruptions date to about 300,000 years ago, though its graceful pre-1980 cone was less than 3,000 years old; and Mount Baker began around 140,000 years ago, with most of its cone built 40,000-12,000 years ago. Glacier Peak is likewise older than the last ice age. All five are considered active.

events.title: Earlier ice ages: the Double Bluff and Possession glaciations
events.summary: The Vashon ice was only the latest of several Cordilleran ice sheets to fill the Puget Lowland. Sea cliffs on Whidbey Island (Double Bluff, Possession Point) expose older glacial deposits from about 190,000-125,000 and 80,000-60,000 years ago, separated by warm-interval river, lake and peat beds (the Whidbey Formation and the Olympia beds, whose type section is in the bluffs of Discovery Park in Seattle). Each ice sheet reshaped the lowland and buried the one before.

events.title: The Okanogan Lobe dams the Columbia: Glacial Lake Columbia, Grand Coulee and Dry Falls
events.summary: East of the Cascades, tongues of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet filled the Okanogan, Methow, Sanpoil, Colville and Pend Oreille valleys. The Okanogan Lobe spread across the Waterville Plateau to the Withrow Moraine and plugged the Columbia River (19,000-17,000 years ago), backing up Glacial Lake Columbia, which lasted until about 15,000 years ago. Missoula floods pouring into that lake were shunted south through Grand Coulee, cutting the 50-mile canyon and the 3.5-mile-wide, 400-foot Dry Falls between about 17,000 and 14,000 years ago. Spokane sat just beyond the ice, under the path of the floods.

events.title: The Missoula floods carve the Channeled Scablands
events.summary: Again and again - at least 75 times before a Mount St. Helens ash fall 16,000 years ago and 30 or more times after - an ice dam in Idaho broke and Glacial Lake Missoula emptied across eastern Washington in days. The floods stripped the Palouse soil off the Cheney-Palouse tract south of Spokane, scoured the Grand Coulee, Moses Coulee and Quincy Basin, and then jammed at Wallula Gap, pooling as temporary Lake Lewis up to about 1,200-1,250 feet above sea level: the Pasco Basin, the Tri-Cities (under some 800 feet of water), the Yakima Valley to near Yakima, the Walla Walla and Touchet valleys, and the Snake valley past Lewiston were all drowned for days to weeks. The water then roared through the Columbia Gorge past Vancouver to the sea. Western Washington beyond the gorge was untouched.

events.title: The Puget Lobe: the Vashon ice sheet buries Seattle, Tacoma and Olympia
events.when: about 19,000 to 16,000 years ago; maximum about 17,000 years ago
events.summary: A lobe of the Cordilleran Ice Sheet flowed south out of British Columbia, filled the Puget Lowland and reached its limit near Tenino, south of Olympia, about 17,000 years ago. The ice was roughly 5,000 feet thick at Bellingham, about 3,000 feet over Seattle, about 2,000 feet over Tacoma and about 1,000 feet near Olympia. Seattle was under ice for less than 2,000 years, yet the ice left almost everything we see: the north-south ridges of Capitol Hill, Queen Anne and Beacon Hill are glacially streamlined drumlins; the Lawton Clay, Esperance Sand and Vashon till in the Discovery Park bluffs are its deposits; and meltwater under the ice gouged the deep troughs of Puget Sound, Lake Washington and Hood Canal. By about 16,000 years ago the ice front had melted back north of Seattle.

events.title: Glacial Lakes Russell and Bretz: the lowland becomes a lake
events.summary: With the ice plugging the Strait of Juan de Fuca, meltwater could not escape north, so as the glacier advanced and again as it retreated a vast lake filled the lowland south of the ice front. Glacial Lake Russell stretched from the Seattle area to the Black Hills and spilled over the Black Lake divide near Olympia into the Chehalis River and out to Grays Harbor - which is why the Chehalis valley is far too wide for its river. When the ice uncovered Admiralty Inlet, a lower lake, Glacial Lake Bretz, drained north through the Chimacum Valley to Discovery Bay. The lakes' old shorelines and deltas now tilt upward to the north by about a metre per kilometre because the land has rebounded since the ice left.

events.title: Puget Sound is born: the sea floods in and the land rebounds
events.summary: Once the retreating ice opened the Strait, seawater poured into the lowland, floated the remaining ice and dropped shell-bearing glacial-marine mud (the Everson drift of Bellingham, Whidbey and Everett) over the northern and central lowland. The crust, freed of its ice load, then rose quickly - about 35-70 percent of the rebound had already happened by the glacial maximum, and the lowland had lifted out of the sea by roughly 13,000 years ago. Puget Sound, Lake Washington and the islands took their modern outlines over the following millennia as sea level rose worldwide.

events.title: Ice-age giants and the first people: mammoths, mastodons, bison and sloths
events.summary: As the ice and floods receded, Washington was grassland and parkland roamed by Columbian mammoths (the state fossil; one at Coyote Canyon near Kennewick died about 17,000 years ago in Missoula-flood sediments), American mastodons, giant Bison antiquus and Jefferson's ground sloths. Workers digging a light-tower footing at Sea-Tac Airport in 1961 found a ground sloth, radiocarbon-dated to about 12,500-12,700 years (roughly 15,000 calendar years) ago, now mounted at the Burke Museum. On Orcas Island a bison butchered by people about 13,700 years ago (Ayer Pond) and the Manis mastodon at Sequim show humans hunting here within a thousand years of the ice leaving. Most of these giants were extinct by about 11,000 years ago.

events.title: The Manis mastodon: people hunting at Sequim
events.summary: Digging a pond with a backhoe on his Happy Valley farm near Sequim in 1977, Emanuel Manis turned up mastodon tusks. Washington State University's Carl Gustafson found a rib with a sharpened bone point embedded in it - a spear tip made from another mastodon's bone. Redating and CT scanning in 2011 (Waters et al., Science) put the kill at about 13,800 years ago, several centuries before the Clovis culture, making it among the oldest evidence of people anywhere in the Americas and the oldest in Washington. The rib is held by the Washington State Historical Society in Tacoma.

events.title: Glacier Peak's great ash eruptions
events.summary: Washington's most remote volcano produced a burst of nine explosive eruptions within a few centuries, the largest throwing out more than five times the tephra of Mount St. Helens in 1980 - among the biggest Cascade eruptions since the ice age. Ash drifted east over the whole of eastern Washington and on to Montana and beyond; near Chelan the deposit is more than a foot thick, and the layer lies on top of all the Missoula-flood deposits, which is how geologists know the floods had ended. Glacier Peak has erupted several more times since, most recently a few hundred years ago.

events.title: The Osceola Mudflow: Mount Rainier's summit collapses into the lowland
events.region: King and Pierce counties (White and Green river valleys), Puget Lowland
events.summary: An eruption triggered the collapse of Mount Rainier's weakened, clay-rich summit and northeast flank. About 3.8 cubic kilometres of rock turned into a wall of mud that ran more than 70 miles down the White River, buried the Enumclaw plateau and spread across 212 square miles of lowland, reaching Kent, Auburn, Sumner and an arm of Puget Sound at what is now the Port of Tacoma. It is the largest lahar known from Rainier and lopped some 1,000-2,000 feet off the mountain. Kent, Auburn, Enumclaw, Buckley and much of the Kent valley stand on its deposits.

events.title: The Seattle Fault earthquake of 923-924 CE
events.summary: A magnitude 7-7.5 earthquake on the Seattle Fault - the east-west fault under the stadiums, I-90 and Bainbridge Island - lifted Restoration Point and Alki Point about 7 metres (23 feet) out of Puget Sound in an instant while the ground north of the fault, at West Point and Magnolia, dropped about a metre. A tsunami swept sand across West Point and Cultus Bay; hillsides slid into Lake Washington off Mercer Island and near Saint Edward State Park, carrying whole forests that still stand upright under water; and landslides fell into Lake Sammamish. Tree rings, radiocarbon, cosmogenic dating and tribal oral histories pin it to late 923-early 924 CE; a 2023 study found the Saddle Mountain fault near Hood Canal ruptured at the same time, so the combined event could have reached magnitude 7.8. It is the only magnitude 7.5+ crustal quake found here in 11,000 years.

events.title: The Electron Mudflow buries the Puyallup valley
events.region: Orting and the Puyallup valley (Pierce County)
events.summary: Without any eruption, a slab of rotten, hydrothermally altered rock on Mount Rainier's west face (Sunset Amphitheater) let go and became a clay-rich lahar of about 0.26 cubic kilometres. It was 30 metres deep where it left the mountains at Electron and flowed down the Puyallup valley at least as far as Sumner, burying the forest and leaving the flat valley floor that Orting now sits on. Tree-ring and radiocarbon work dates it to about 1507 CE. Because it needed no eruption warning, it is the scenario behind the Puyallup valley's lahar sirens and Orting's evacuation drills.

events.title: The great Cascadia earthquake of January 26, 1700
events.summary: The whole Cascadia subduction zone, some 1,000 km from Vancouver Island to northern California, ruptured in a magnitude ~9 earthquake. The outer coast dropped 1-2 metres in moments, drowning forests in salt water - the ghost cedars of the Copalis River and Willapa Bay died in the winter of 1699-1700 by tree-ring count - and a tsunami tens of feet high swept the coast and, ten hours later, Japan, where villagers recorded an 'orphan' tsunami with no felt quake. Native oral histories recall the shaking and the waves. Willapa Bay marshes record seven such quakes in 3,500 years and deep-sea turbidites 19 in 10,000 years, averaging about 500 years apart.

events.title: The 1872 North Cascades (Chelan-Entiat) earthquake

A landslide at Ribbon Cliff dammed the Columbia River for hours, hot springs changed, and settlers and Native people reported ground cracks and geysering sand. Lidar has since revealed a fresh 1-2 metre scarp on the Spencer Canyon fault southwest of Entiat, the likely source, and the Entiat earthquake cluster still active today may be its aftershocks.

events.title: The 1949 Olympia earthquake
events.summary: A deep (about 50 km) earthquake inside the sinking Juan de Fuca plate, centered between Olympia and Tacoma, shook western Washington at magnitude 7.1 (some modern recalculations give 6.7) - the strongest in the region's recorded history. Eight people died, including schoolchildren struck by falling masonry, and dozens were seriously hurt; the Capitol dome in Olympia, downtown Seattle and Tacoma buildings and dozens of schools were damaged. It was the first of three deep 'Benioff' quakes (1949, 1965, 2001) that define the Puget Sound region's most frequent big-earthquake type.

events.title: Mount St. Helens erupts
events.summary: A magnitude 5.1 earthquake set off the largest landslide in recorded history, uncorking a sideways blast that flattened 230 square miles of forest, followed by a nine-hour ash column 15 miles high and lahars that choked the Toutle and Cowlitz rivers and the Columbia shipping channel. Fifty-seven people died. The ash cloud blacked out Yakima within an hour and Spokane by afternoon, closed I-90 under inches of grit at Ritzville and dusted eleven states; the mountain lost 1,300 feet of its summit. Washington's volcanoes went from scenery to hazard overnight, and the Cascades Volcano Observatory was founded to watch them.

events.title: Today: Washington rides the leading edge of a subduction zone
events.when: the last ~30 million years, and now
events.summary: Offshore, the small Juan de Fuca plate - the last fragment of the ancient Farallon plate - is sliding northeast under Washington at 3-4 cm per year, about half its speed of 7 million years ago. That sinking slab feeds the Cascade volcanoes, flexes the coast, generates slow 'tremor' episodes under Puget Sound every 14 months or so, and stores the strain for magnitude-9 Cascadia earthquakes (last one 1700; average spacing about 500 years). At the same time the Oregon coast block rotates clockwise and squeezes western Washington northward against Canada, loading the shallow Seattle, Tacoma and other crustal faults.

events.title: Fifty million years from now (a qualitative projection)
events.when: about 50 million years in the future
events.summary: Nobody can map this precisely, but the trends are clear. The Juan de Fuca plate is shrinking and breaking into pieces; most geologists expect subduction here to die out within tens of millions of years, as it already has off California, leaving a San Andreas-style sliding boundary and quieting the Cascade volcanoes. North America will keep drifting west-southwest at a couple of centimetres a year - roughly 1,000 km over 50 million years - carrying Seattle with it, while Baja California and Los Angeles slide north past the coast toward Alaska. Puget Sound, the Olympics and even Mount Rainier are fleeting: in 50 million years they will have been eroded, filled or rebuilt many times over, as the whole 40-million-year life of the Cascade arc has been shorter than this span.

errors.event_title: The Seattle Fault earthquake of 923-924 CE
errors.problem: Says the quake 'lifted Restoration Point and Alki Point about 7 metres'. Only Restoration Point rose ~7 m; Alki Point rose about 4 m (Bucknam et al. 1992; City of Seattle best-available-science summary: 'as much as 7 m at Restoration Point', 'over 4 m at Alki Point', 1-1.5 m subsidence at West Point).
errors.correction: '...lifted Restoration Point on Bainbridge Island about 7 metres (23 feet) and Alki Point about 4 metres (13 feet) out of Puget Sound in an instant, while the ground north of the fault at West Point dropped 1-1.5 metres.'

errors.event_title: The Seattle Fault earthquake of 923-924 CE
errors.problem: 'It is the only magnitude 7.5+ crustal quake found here in 11,000 years' is unsupported. The published record: Toe Jam Hill trenches on Bainbridge Island show three or possibly four ~M7 Seattle Fault earthquakes between about 2,500 and 1,000 years ago (Nelson et al. 2003), and marsh studies show metre-scale uplift happened only once in the last ~7,500 years (Sherrod). Nobody has published an 11,000-year catalogue of M7.5+ crustal quakes for the region.
errors.correction: 'It is the only time in at least 7,500 years that the Seattle Fault lifted the shoreline by metres; trenches on Bainbridge Island record three or four smaller (about magnitude 7) Seattle Fault quakes between roughly 2,500 and 1,000 years ago.'

errors.event_title: The Seattle Fault earthquake of 923-924 CE
errors.problem: 'Tree rings, radiocarbon, cosmogenic dating and tribal oral histories pin it to late 923-early 924 CE' overstates what oral histories contribute. The 923-924 date comes from tree-ring crossdating plus the 774-775 CE cosmic-ray spike preserved in the rings (Black et al. 2023); Coast Salish a'yahos stories are tied to places along the fault but do not give a calendar date. Also the dating is 'cosmogenic radiation pulse' in tree rings, not cosmogenic-nuclide surface dating.
errors.correction: 'Tree rings - anchored by a cosmic-ray spike of 774-775 CE recorded in the wood - pin the quake to between the growing seasons of 923 and 924 CE (Black et al. 2023). Coast Salish oral traditions of a'yahos, a shaking serpent-spirit, are tied to places along the fault (Ludwin et al. 2005).'

errors.event_title: Puget Sound is born: the sea floods in and the land rebounds
errors.problem: 'About 35-70 percent of the rebound had already happened by the glacial maximum' misreads Thorson (1981). Thorson's statement is that 35-70 percent of isostatic EQUILIBRIUM (i.e., of the downward crustal depression under the ice load) had been attained by the glacial maximum. Rebound cannot precede deglaciation.
errors.correction: 'The crust had sunk only part way - about 35-70 percent of the way to full equilibrium under the ice load (Thorson 1981) - and once the ice left it rose quickly; maximum postglacial uplift reached about 140 m in the northern lowland, and the lowland had lifted out of the sea by roughly 13,000 years ago.'

errors.event_title: Earlier ice ages: the Double Bluff and Possession glaciations
errors.problem: Says the Olympia beds' 'type section is in the bluffs of Discovery Park in Seattle'. No such type section exists: 'Olympia beds' is an informal name (Minard & Booth 1988) for deposits of the Olympia nonglacial interval of Armstrong et al. (1965). The units whose type sections are at Fort Lawton/Discovery Park are the Lawton Clay and Esperance Sand (Mullineaux et al. 1965).
errors.correction: '...separated by warm-interval river, lake and peat beds (the Whidbey Formation and the Olympia beds, which are well exposed at the base of the Discovery Park bluffs in Seattle, below the Lawton Clay whose type section is there).'

errors.event_title: The Missoula floods carve the Channeled Scablands
errors.problem: 'Western Washington beyond the gorge was untouched' contradicts the preceding sentence ('past Vancouver') and the record: floodwater ponded in the Portland Basin to roughly 400 ft (120 m), drowning the Clark County lowlands (Vancouver, Camas, Washougal) and backing up tributary valleys, before continuing to the Pacific. The applicability rule in the caveats (Lake Lewis/scabland only) is fine, but this sentence would mislead Clark County visitors.
errors.correction: 'West of the gorge the water spread across the Portland Basin, putting Vancouver, Camas and Washougal under hundreds of feet of water before it ran on to the sea; the Puget Lowland and the outer coast were untouched.'

errors.event_title: Columbia River Basalt floods bury a third of Washington
errors.problem: '90% erupted 16.5-15.6 Ma' is an older figure. High-precision U-Pb dating (Kasbohm & Schoene 2018, Science Advances) shows more than 95% of the CRBG erupted between 16.7 and 15.9 Ma - a span of under 800,000 years, consistent with the event's own 16.7 Ma start date.

Mount Adams (520,000 yr), the present Mount Rainier (500,000 yr) and Mount St. Helens (about 300,000 yr) are as old as or older than Homo sapiens (~300,000 yr) and far younger than the genus Homo (~2.8 million yr); only Mount Baker (140,000 yr) is clearly younger than our species. factcheck.missing_events: Candidates visitors in those places would expect, grouped by where they matter. (1) Holocene volcanic activity, currently a gap between 'volcanoes are born' and 1980: Mount St. Helens' Yn ash (~3,900 yr ago, the thickest Holocene ash over much of eastern WA) and its 1800 'T' eruption and 1840s-50s activity; Mount Baker's 6,700-yr collapse/lahar into the Nooksack and Baker valleys and its 1843 eruption and 1975 Sherman Crater steaming; Mount Rainier's National Lahar (~2,200 yr, Nisqually valley), Round Pass Mudflow (~2,600 yr), the ~1,000-yr-old pyroclastic flows, and the 1947 Kautz Creek debris flow; Mount Adams' ~1,000-yr lavas and 1921 avalanche; Mount St. Helens' 2004-2008 dome-building eruption. (2) Bonneville landslide / 'Bridge of the Gods' (c. 1450 CE): a Table Mountain collapse dammed the Columbia near Stevenson-Cascade Locks, drowned forests upstream, and is remembered in Klickitat/Columbia River tribes' oral tradition - essential for Skamania and Clark counties. (3) Oso (SR 530) landslide, March 22, 2014, 43 people killed - Snohomish County's defining recent geologic event; needs care in wording (see notes). (4) Sucia Island dinosaur (San Juan County): Washington's only dinosaur fossil, an ~80-million-year-old theropod femur found 2012, named the state dinosaur ('Suciasaurus rex') in 2023. (5) Richey-Clovis cache, East Wenatchee (found 1987, ~13,000 yr): the largest Clovis points ever found, directly relevant to the 'first people' event; Marmes Rockshelter (Franklin County, ~11,000 yr, flooded by Lower Monumental Dam 1969); Lind Coulee (Grant County, ~11,000-12,000 yr); and, handled with care, the Ancient One/Kennewick Man (~8,500-9,000 yr, reburied by Columbia Plateau tribes in 2017). (6) Alpine (Cascade and Olympic) glaciation, including the Evans Creek stade (~22-18 ka) and the carving of Lake Chelan (1,486 ft deep, below sea level) and the Yakima, Wenatchee and Methow valleys - the Vashon/Puget Lobe story covers only the lowland. (7) Palouse loess (~2 million yr to present) and the Ringold Formation / ancestral Columbia River (~8-3 Ma; White Bluffs) for Whitman, Franklin and Benton counties; the diversion of the ancestral Columbia by basalt flows (Miocene) and the folding of the Yakima fold belt (Pliocene-present) as a separate event. (8) Bonneville Flood (~17,500 yr), which came down the Snake River past Lewiston-Clarkston and Asotin County. (9) Mima Mounds (Thurston County), a visitor magnet with an unresolved origin. (10) Historic quakes beyond the five listed: 1936 Milton-Freewater (M6.1, Walla Walla area), 1946 Vancouver Island M7.3 felt across Puget Sound, and the 1939 and 1946 Puget Sound deep quakes. (11) Science-history milestones that place-visitors ask about: J Harlen Bretz proposes the Spokane/Missoula floods (1923) and is vindicated (1960s); 1992 discovery of the Seattle Fault's 1,100-yr quake (already partially covered via HistoryLink 9388). (12) The Glacial Lake Carbon/Lake Puyallup and the lowland tsunami record (Cultus Bay, West Point) could be folded into existing events.
factcheck.sensitivity_notes: (1) Event 'Ice-age giants and the first people': 'the first people' and 'humans hunting here within a thousand years of the ice leaving' read as if people simply 'arrived'; many Washington tribes hold that they have been here since time immemorial and that these ancestors are their own. Suggested: title 'Ice-age giants and the earliest known people', and text '...the Manis mastodon at Sequim show that people - ancestors of today's tribes - were hunting here within a thousand years of the ice leaving.' Consider a short standing line for the human-history rings: 'The tribes of Washington have lived here since time immemorial; archaeological dates are minimum ages, not arrival dates.' (2) Event 'The Manis mastodon': 'the oldest trace of humans in Washington' -> 'the oldest known trace of people in Washington'; add that the site lies in the traditional territory of the Jamestown S'Klallam Tribe (Sequim) and link to the tribe's site. For Ayer Pond on Orcas Island, note the Lummi, Samish, Swinomish and Tulalip ancestral ties if a tribal link is added. (3) Event 'Mazama ash': 'Indigenous oral traditions in the region recall the eruption' -> name them: 'Klamath oral tradition (southern Oregon) recalls the eruption'. (4) Event 'Seattle Fault 923-924': replace 'tribal oral histories' with 'Coast Salish oral traditions (Suquamish, Duwamish and neighbouring peoples) of a'yahos, the shaking serpent-spirit, are tied to places along the fault (Ludwin et al. 2005)'; do not present them as dating evidence (see error above). (5) Event 'Cascadia 1700': 'Native oral histories recall the shaking and the waves' -> 'Oral histories of coastal nations - Makah, Quileute, Hoh, Quinault and others - recall the shaking and the waves (Ludwin et al. 2005, Seismological Research Letters)'. The closing line 'The next one is a matter of when, not if' is standard WA EMD phrasing but consider adding a preparedness link (mil.wa.gov) so the fear has an outlet. (6) Event '1872 earthquake': 'settlers and Native people' is acceptable; if more specific, 'Indigenous residents at Lake Chelan and along the Columbia (ancestors of today's Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation)'. (7) Event 'Electron Mudflow': the 2025 USGS data release notes 'Indigenous narratives about the mudflow'; the Puyallup Tribe's territory covers the deposit - consider 'The Puyallup Tribe's territory includes this valley' and avoid 'buried the forest' with no human mention when the valley was inhabited. (8) Volcano names: consider giving Indigenous names alongside English ones where documented (Tahoma/Təqʷuʔməʔ for Rainier; Loowit/Lawetlat'la for St. Helens, Cowlitz and Yakama; Pahto for Adams; Kulshan/Koma Kulshan for Baker; Dakobed for Glacier Peak), linking to the respective tribal nations. (9) Tragedy wording: 1949 'schoolchildren struck by falling masonry' is accurate (Marvin Klegman, 11, Tacoma, and Jack Roller, a Castle Rock High School senior) and restrained - keep; 'Fifty-seven people died' for 1980 is fine. If the 2014 Oso landslide is added, state plainly 'forty-three people died' and avoid 'deadliest'/'record' framing; link to the Snohomish County memorial. For the Ancient One/Kennewick Man, if added, use 'the Ancient One' first, note the 2017 reburial by the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, Yakama Nation, Nez Perce, Umatilla and Wanapum, and do not show skeletal images. (10) Event 'Mount St. Helens erupts': 'Washington's volcanoes went from scenery to hazard overnight' is fine; consider adding that the mountain is sacred to the Cowlitz Tribe and Yakama Nation.

caveats: Dates use the site convention: start_years_ago = 2000 - year (so 1889 = 111, 2020 = -20). HistoryLink.org essays (CC BY-NC-ND) are the primary citations: link out and summarize, never copy prose; Wikipedia prose is CC BY-SA and must be quoted with attribution if shown. Known source disagreements: Heceta landing July 12 vs 14, 1775; Medicine Creek ratification Mar 3 vs Apr 10, 1855; Walla Walla treaty signing dates (June 9 Yakama/Umatilla, June 11 Nez Perce); Ballard annexation May 19 vs 29, 1907; Manis site age 13,800-13,900 cal BP (older 12,000 figure is superseded); Marmes age ~11,000 (older reports said up to 13,000); 1949 quake magnitude 6.7-7.1; 2021 heat-dome deaths 78-157 direct, 400+ with indirect. 'Founded' for cities is ambiguous (first settler vs plat vs incorporation); events give both where known. Tribal homeland events describe living nations whose territories overlap and are not exhausted by reservation boundaries; several nations (Duwamish, Chinook, Wanapum, Steilacoom, Snohomish) are not federally recognized, and recognition status should be re-checked before publishing. Lat/lon are approximate centroids for the place named, not exact event spots. Earliest-presence dates are calibrated calendar years; the site should present them as 'about' values. Umatilla and Nez Perce are headquartered in Oregon and Idaho but hold ceded and usual-and-accustomed lands in SE Washington. The 20 largest cities are per the 2020 census (Seattle, Spokane, Tacoma, Vancouver, Bellevue, Kent, Everett, Renton, Spokane Valley, Federal Way, Yakima, Kirkland, Bellingham, Auburn, Kennewick, Pasco, Redmond, Marysville, Sammamish, Lakewood); Olympia is added as the capital.

errors.event_title: Spaniards land at Point Grenville
errors.problem: Two factual problems in the summary: (1) 'Days later Quinault warriors killed seven of Bodega y Quadra's men near Destruction Island' is wrong on both timing and place. The cited HistoryLink essay says the Sonora's seven-man wood-and-water party was killed the SAME day as Hezeta's landing, on the beach near the landing site; Hezeta named the point Punta de los Mártires (Point of the Martyrs), which is Point Grenville itself. Destruction Island (named by Meares/Barkley for the 1787 killing of Barkley's crew at the Hoh River) is 30 miles north and unrelated to the 1775 killings. (2) The 'when' leads with July 14, but the entry's own primary source (HistoryLink 5690) and Wikipedia's Point Grenville article both give July 12, 1775, so the cited evidence contradicts the headline date. Also the second source (sos.wa.gov/legacy/timeline/detail.aspx?id=6) now redirects to a generic Legacy Washington page with no 1775 content.
errors.correction: when: 'July 12, 1775 (some sources July 14)'. Summary: '...the first recorded European landing in Washington. The same day Quinault fighters killed seven of Bodega y Quadra's crew from the Sonora who had gone ashore for water and wood, and Hezeta named the headland Punta de los Mártires; Juan Pérez had sighted the coast the year before.' Replace the SOS timeline link with HistoryLink 5688 (expedition overview) and/or Wikipedia Point Grenville.

errors.event_title: Wave of suburban incorporations

HistoryLink attributes the Federal Way vote to residents' frustration with King County's failure to regulate growth, not to the GMA.

factcheck.missing_events:
Everything below was checked for existence, not every date; verify before adding. Grouped by why it matters for a parcel-level Washington place-history site.

LANDSCAPE-CHANGING ENGINEERING (changes what is literally under a given address): Seattle and Tacoma tideflat fills and Harbor Island (1909, then the largest artificial island); Duwamish River straightening (1913-17); White River diverted into the Puyallup after the 1906 flood (made permanent 1914) and Cedar River diverted into Lake Washington (1912), which remade the Kent-Auburn-Renton valley; Green Lake lowered (1911); Mud Mountain Dam (1948) and Howard Hanson Dam (1962) ending Green/White River floods; Sammamish River channelized (1960s); Columbia River floods of 1894 and 1948; Chehalis/I-5 floods 2007. ASARCO Tacoma Smelter (1890-1985) and its arsenic/lead plume over ~1,000 sq mi of the Puget Sound lowland (WA Ecology Dirt Alert) is probably the single most parcel-relevant omission; likewise Commencement Bay (1983) and Lower Duwamish (2001) Superfund listings and the 1989 Hanford Tri-Party Agreement.

COLUMBIA/SNAKE DAMS beyond Grand Coulee and The Dalles: Rock Island (1933, first dam on the Columbia), Bonneville (1938), McNary (1954), Chief Joseph (1955), Priest Rapids (1959) and Wanapum (1963, which forced the Wanapum village to move), Rocky Reach (1961), Wells (1967), Ice Harbor (1962) through Lower Granite (1975) on the Snake (flooding Marmes, Lyons Ferry, Palus sites), Columbia River Treaty (1964); Snoqualmie Falls power plant (1898); PUD movement (1930s); 1949 Hanford 'Green Run' and downwinders.

EARLY TOWNS/PLACES NOT COVERED: Port Townsend (1851, customs port 1854), Steilacoom (1854, first incorporated town), Port Gamble mill (1853, Pope & Talbot), Port Blakely mill (1864, once world's largest sawmill), Ebey's Landing/Whidbey (1850; Isaac Ebey killed 1857), Walla Walla incorporated 1862 (largest town in the territory into the 1870s), Centralia founded 1875 by George Washington (a Black founder), Longview planned city (1923), Richland as Hanford's government town (1943-58), Bremerton/Puget Sound Naval Shipyard (1891), Camp/Fort Lewis (1917), McChord Field (1938), NAS Whidbey (1942), Bangor Trident base (1977), Naval Station Everett (1994).

INDIGENOUS HISTORY GAPS (important to balance the treaty-and-war framing): Tansy Point treaties of 1851 (Chinook and Clatsop signed with Anson Dart; never ratified, which is why 'never signed a treaty' needs nuance for the Chinook); Smohalla and the Washani/Dreamer religion at Priest Rapids (Wanapum) and the Indian Shaker Church founded by John Slocum at Mud Bay (1882), two religions born in Washington; Chief Moses and the Columbia (Moses) Reservation (1879-84); Wenatchi loss of the Wenatshapam fishery (1894); allotment under the Dawes Act (1887) and the breakup of the Puyallup (1893 land sales), Yakama and Colville reservations; Indian boarding schools (Tulalip 1857/1905, Cushman at Tacoma, Fort Spokane 1900, Chemawa); 1862 smallpox epidemic; Fort Lawton occupation (1970) and Daybreak Star (1977) in Seattle; Centennial Accord (1989); Puyallup Land Claims Settlement (1990, $162 million); Rafeedie shellfish decision (1994) and the culverts case (U.S. v. Washington, affirmed by the Supreme Court 2018); Tse-whit-zen village uncovered at Port Angeles (2003-04); Lummi defeat of the Cherry Point coal terminal (2016); Lushootseed revival (Vi Hilbert); Duwamish Longhouse (2009).

RESOURCE ECONOMY: first salmon cannery on the Columbia at Eagle Cliff, Wahkiakum County (1866, Hume brothers); Weyerhaeuser's 1900 purchase of 900,000 acres from the Northern Pacific; coal towns Newcastle, Black Diamond, Roslyn (1888 strike and Black miners; 1892 Roslyn disaster, 45 dead) and Carbonado/Wilkeson; Yakima Project (1905) and Wenatchee Highline Canal (1903) that created the apple districts; Palouse wheat; Washington wine (Ste. Michelle 1967); Bracero program and the growth of Mexican American communities in the Yakima Valley (1940s on) and the Chateau Ste. Michelle/UFW contract (1995); Japanese American farms (Bellevue, Kent, Bainbridge) and their 1942 loss is mentioned but Nihonmachi/Japantown is not; Filipino cannery union and the 1981 Domingo-Viernes murders.

DISASTERS AND EPIDEMICS: 1872 North Cascades earthquake (M6.5-7, largest crustal quake in state history); Yacolt Burn (1902, 38 dead, largest WA fire until 2014); 1910 Big Burn (NE WA/Idaho); 1918 influenza (about 5,000 Washington deaths; Seattle mask order); Carlton Complex (2014, largest wildfire in state history), Okanogan Complex (2015), Labor Day 2020 fires (Malden destroyed); Inauguration Day storm (1993), Hanukkah Eve storm (2006); Hood Canal Bridge sinking (1979); Deception Pass Bridge (1935).

TRANSPORT/URBAN FORM: Seattle's electric streetcars (1889, first on the West Coast) and the Seattle-Tacoma (1902) and Seattle-Everett (1910) interurbans; Pacific Highway/US 99 and the Sunset Highway over Snoqualmie Pass (1915); Stevens Pass highway (1925); North Cascades Highway (1972); Washington State Ferries created from the Black Ball buyout (1951); Sea-Tac Airport (1944/1949) and Boeing Field (1928); Northgate (1950, first regional 'mall'), Bellevue Square (1946), Southcenter (1968); Seattle bus tunnel (1990); Tacoma Dome (1983); Seattle racial restrictive covenants and the 1968 open-housing ordinance (parcel-level: covenants are in deeds across the state); Hooverville on the Seattle tideflats (1931-41); CHOP/Capitol Hill protest zone (2020).

INSTITUTIONS AND POLITICS: Washington Agricultural College/WSU (1890, opened 1892), Whitman College (1859/1882), Gonzaga (1887), Western/Central/Eastern normal schools (1890s), Evergreen (1967); statewide Prohibition (Jan 1, 1916); initiative and referendum (1912); Dixy Lee Ray first woman governor (1976); Gary Locke first Chinese American governor (1996); Shoreline Management Act (1971); Referendum 74 and Initiative 502 (2012); Boeing 707/Dash 80 (1954), B-17 (1935), Kaiser Vancouver shipyards (1942); Boeing moves HQ out of Seattle (2001); Starbucks (1971), Costco (1983), Nordstrom (1901), REI (1938); Mount Baker steam crisis (1975); Spokane Garry and the 1838 Tshimakain and 1839 Cowlitz missions (first churches north of the Columbia).
factcheck.sensitivity_notes: 1) Chief Seattle's name: 'si?al' is an ASCII stand-in; use the Lushootseed spelling siʔaɬ (Wikipedia and the Suquamish Tribe use it). 2) 'Your spot is on the traditional land of the {tribe}; their descendants live here today' implies the nation is in the past; use 'the {tribe}, who live here today' or 'whose people still live here'. 3) Hood Canal event: 'All trace to the Point No Point Treaty of 1855' makes the nations sound as if they began with the treaty; say 'All three nations' reservations and treaty rights trace to the Point No Point Treaty of 1855; the peoples themselves have been here since time immemorial.' 4) Puget Sound War: besides the Leschi attribution (see errors), 'neutral tribes were interned on islands' is good but could add that most Puyallup, Nisqually and Squaxin families were confined on Fox Island under guard; also prefer 'Native fighters' or 'warriors from the tribes' over 'Nisqually, Puyallup, Muckleshoot and Klickitat fighters led by Leschi'. 5) Leschi: 'convicted of murdering a militia colonel in wartime' should say 'convicted of murder for the wartime killing of militiaman A. Benton Moses, a death the 2004 historical court ruled was an act of war, not a crime' so the entry doesn't restate the discredited charge. 6) Steptoe/Wright: 'hanged Qualchan and others' should note these were summary executions without trial (Wright hanged about 16 men in September 1858, Qualchan within minutes of arriving under a flag of truce); 'Resistance on the Plateau collapsed' reads as triumphal; prefer 'Armed resistance on the Plateau ended'. 7) Battle of Seattle: 'several hundred Native fighters from east of the lake attacked' is fine, but the at_your_spot line about cannon fire landing 'here' is playful about a deadly event; keep neutral ('Shells from the Decatur fell on this ground'). 8) Tacoma expulsion at_your_spot: 'driven out at gunpoint' is not in the cited source (HistoryLink describes a mob forcing people out, in the rain, to the rail siding); use 'driven out by a mob' or 'marched out of town by a mob'. 9) Auburn at_your_spot: 'Your spot was in a town literally named Slaughter' is flip given it commemorates a death in the Puget Sound War; suggest 'Your spot was in a town named Slaughter, for an Army lieutenant killed in the 1855-56 war, until 1893.' 10) Japanese Americans: replace 'removed' and 'sent through Camp Harmony ... to Minidoka' with 'forcibly removed and incarcerated' and 'held at the Puyallup fairgrounds (Camp Harmony) before incarceration at Minidoka' (Densho/NPS style; avoid 'internment' for citizens); the at_your_spot 'given days to leave' is fine. 11) Smallpox: 'abandoned villages strewn with bones' is Vancouver's own observation but is graphic; consider 'and abandoned villages' with the bones detail left to the source. 12) Whitman: 'a group killed the Whitmans and 11 others' is good and avoids 'massacre' (keep); consider adding that five Cayuse men were hanged in Oregon City in 1850 so the entry doesn't end only with Native violence. 13) Ozette: 'preserving 55,000 everyday objects' is fine; add that the Makah Tribe co-directed the dig and owns the collection (Makah Cultural and Research Center), which is already partly stated. 14) Lower Columbia event: 'the traders who met Gray and Lewis and Clark; still denied federal recognition' is fine, but add 'signed the unratified 1851 Tansy Point treaties' so 'never signed Stevens' 1855 treaty terms' is not read as 'never made a treaty'. 15) Makah whaling: 'amid protests' is neutral;
